47891.etyen:
Borrowed from German Rheinländer (“Rhinelander; reinlender dance”), originally “a person from the Rhineland”, from Rheinland (“Rhineland”) and the inhabitant-forming suffix -er, with umlaut. The dance name literally denotes a dance associated with the Rhineland.
German Rheinland is from Rhein (“Rhine”) + Land (“land, country”). Rhein (“Rhine”) is inherited from Old High German Rīn (“Rhine”), from Proto-West Germanic *Rīn, from Proto-Germanic *Rīnaz, ultimately from Gaulish Gaulish Rēnos, from Proto-Celtic *reinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reyH- (“to move, flow, run”).
Doublet of rhinlender

1000467.etyen:
Variant of Anne, itself a variant of Anna. First attested in the 15th century. The Christian name tradition ultimately continues Latin Anna, from Ancient Greek Ἄννα (Ánna), from Biblical Hebrew Biblical Hebrew חַנָּה (Ḥannāh, “grace, favour”), from חָנַן (ḥānan, “to be gracious, show favour”). Doublet of Hannah (“female given name”).
The Biblical Hebrew name חַנָּה (Ḥannāh) is borne in the Hebrew Bible by Hannah, the mother of Samuel. Its Greek form Ἄννα (Ánna) occurs in the New Testament as the name of Anna the Prophetess, and the name tradition subsequently became widespread in Christian Eur

1005075.etyen: From fysj (“yuck, ugh”), with an expressive ending of uncertain origin. Det Norske Akademis ordbok suggests that the form may have been modelled on bråttom (“in a hurry”). Store norske leksikon additionally suggests that it may have arisen humorously during the Samnorsk debates of the 1950s, with -om imitating older Norwegian Nynorsk dative forms; alternatively, it may likewise have been influenced by Swedish bråttom (“in a hurry”).
